clinicalPearls: NTM (also termed atypical, environmental, or mycobacteria other than tuberculosis) are ubiquitous in soil and water and refer to mycobacteria other than M. tuberculosis and its close relatives and M. leprae; over 199 species are recognized (p.1414).

Most NTM cause human disease only when host defense is impaired (e.g., bronchiectasis) or breached by inoculation (liposuction, trauma, cardiac surgery); human-to-human transmission is rare and occurs almost exclusively in cystic fibrosis (p.1414).

Pulmonary disease is by far the most common form in North America and is highly associated with pulmonary epithelial defects but NOT with systemic immunodeficiency; disseminated disease instead denotes significant immune dysfunction such as advanced HIV (p.1414, 1416).

Pulmonary MAC most commonly presents in the 6th-7th decade in women with months to years of nagging intermittent cough and fatigue; pulmonary NTM in a tall, thin woman with chest-wall abnormalities is termed 'Lady Windermere syndrome' (p.1416).

Pulmonary MAC affects older nonsmoking white women more than men (onset ~60 years); such patients tend to be taller and thinner with high rates of scoliosis, mitral valve prolapse, and pectus anomalies (p.1416).

Male smokers with upper-lobe cavitary disease tend to carry the same single MAC strain indefinitely, whereas nonsmoking women with nodular bronchiectasis carry several MAC strains simultaneously that change over the disease course (p.1416).
M. kansasii can produce a clinical syndrome strongly resembling tuberculosis with hemoptysis, chest pain, and cavitary lung disease (p.1416).

Disseminated MAC (or M. kansasii) in advanced HIV is now uncommon in North America owing to effective prophylaxis and improved HIV treatment; when common, the portal of entry was the bowel with spread to bone marrow and bloodstream (p.1415).

Disseminated NTM is often indolent and progressive over weeks to months with malaise, fever, weight loss, organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and anemia; blood cultures may be negative even though involved organs carry heavy organism burdens, sometimes with grossly impaired granulomatous response (p.1415).

Isolated cervical lymphadenopathy is the most common form of NTM infection in young children in North America (usually MAC); the swelling is firm and relatively painless with few systemic signs and is often diagnosed inadvertently at biopsy for suspected malignancy (p.1416).
Children with isolated cervical or intrathoracic NTM infection do NOT commonly have underlying immune defects and usually do NOT go on to develop other opportunistic infections (p.1416).

Cutaneous NTM usually requires a break in the skin; rapidly growing NTM (M. abscessus, M. fortuitum, M. chelonae) cause outbreaks via contaminated surgical instruments/injections, with painful erythematous draining subcutaneous nodules typically WITHOUT fever or systemic symptoms (p.1416).

M. marinum (fish tanks, pools, fish handling) causes 'fish-tank granuloma' and can spread up the arm in a sporotrichoid pattern; M. ulcerans causes painless Buruli ulcer via the toxin mycolactone (p.1416).
'Hot-tub lung' is a pulmonary hypersensitivity reaction to NTM (most often MAC) growing in underchlorinated water, distinct from true pulmonary or disseminated infection (p.1415).

For susceptibility testing, only MAC testing for clarithromycin and M. kansasii testing for rifampin is indicated; few data support other in vitro susceptibility tests, and MAC isolates not previously exposed to macrolides are almost always susceptible (p.1417).
harrison.pathophysiology: NTM are ubiquitous environmental organisms (soil and water) with specific niches (e.g., M. simiae in aquifers, M. fortuitum in pedicure baths, M. immunogenum in metalworking fluids). Because exposure is essentially universal yet disease is rare, normal host defenses are strong and significant disease implies a specific susceptibility. Mycobacteria are phagocytosed by macrophages, which release IL-12; IL-12 activates T and NK cells (via STAT4) to secrete IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages/neutrophils (via STAT1) and upregulates TNF-alpha, forming a positive IFN-gamma/IL-12 feedback loop critical for mycobacterial control. Disseminated NTM correlates with declining CD4+ T cells (advanced HIV, idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia), TNF-alpha inhibitors (which impair granuloma formation), Mendelian mutations in the IFN-gamma/IL-12 pathway (IFNG, IFNGR1, IFNGR2, STAT1, GATA2, ISG15, IRF8, IL-12A, IL-12RB1, IL-12RB2, CYBB, IKBKG/NEMO and others), or neutralizing anti-IFN-gamma autoantibodies. Only ~70% of non-HIV disseminated cases have a genetic diagnosis. In contrast, the best-recognized substrate for pulmonary NTM is bronchiectasis (cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, STAT3 hyper-IgE/Job's syndrome, idiopathic), but the mechanism by which bronchiectasis predisposes to locally destructive yet non-systemic disease is unknown (p.1414-1415).
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary tuberculosis (M. kansasii closely mimics TB; PPD/IGRA cross-reactivity)
Malignancy (painless cervical adenopathy in children; isolated intrathoracic NTM mistaken for cancer)
Bronchiectasis exacerbation / underlying structural lung disease
Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (predisposes to NTM and Nocardia)
Sporotrichosis (sporotrichoid spread mimicked by M. marinum)
infectionMimics: M. tuberculosis (clinical, radiographic, and AFB-smear overlap)
Nocardia (gram-positive beaded filamentous rods; alveolar proteinosis predisposes to both)
Sporothrix schenckii (sporotrichoid ascending nodules akin to M. marinum)
nonInfectiousMimics: Malignancy presenting as painless cervical or intrathoracic adenopathy
Hot-tub lung (hypersensitivity pneumonitis-type reaction to NTM rather than invasive infection)
additionalInvestigations: Acid-fast or fluorochrome smears of sputum or body fluids (organisms may appear as beaded gram-positive rods at high burden, but this is unreliable)
Mycobacterial culture using separate processing and dedicated blood culture media; differentiate rapidly growing (<7 days) from slowly growing (>=7 days) species; some labs hold cultures 6 weeks

Liquid culture media for faster isolation; lower incubation temperature (30C) for M. marinum, M. haemophilum, M. ulcerans; special additives (iron/blood for M. haemophilum, mycobactin J for M. genavense)
Species-level identification by biochemical tests, nucleic acid probes/sequencing, HPLC or mass spectrometry; molecular detection for noncultivable species (e.g., M. tilburgii)
Chest CT (tree-in-bud bronchiolar pattern, lingular and right-middle-lobe involvement, bronchiectasis, cavitation)
IGRA (note M. marinum, M. kansasii, M. szulgai carry ESAT6/CFP10 and may cause false-positive IGRA; IGRA is indeterminate with anti-IFN-gamma autoantibodies)
Genetic evaluation of the IFN-gamma/IL-12 pathway and screening for anti-IFN-gamma autoantibodies in disseminated disease without iatrogenic cause; GATA2 evaluation when myelodysplasia coexists
redFlags: Disseminated involvement of two or more organs without an iatrogenic cause (prompts IFN-gamma/IL-12 pathway genetic investigation)
Disseminated NTM with bacterial/viral infections plus conical/peg/missing teeth or abnormal hair pattern in males (suggests NEMO/IKBKG NF-kB defect, possibly with immunoglobulin defects)
Mycobacterial disease with myelodysplasia (investigate GATA2 deficiency)
Disseminated MAC and rapidly growing NTM with other opportunistic infections (e.g., Talaromyces), especially in East Asian women (anti-IFN-gamma autoantibodies)
Infected indwelling IV catheters/lines (M. abscessus, M. fortuitum from contaminated water) requiring catheter removal
harrison.prognosis: NTM cause chronic infections evolving slowly over weeks to years, so emergent therapy before diagnosis and speciation is rarely needed. Treatment is complex, often poorly tolerated, and potentially toxic; inadequate single-drug therapy is almost always associated with emergence of resistance and relapse. Pulmonary MAC therapy is prolonged, generally continued for 12 months after culture conversion (typically at least 18 months total). The typical lag between symptom onset and diagnosis is about 5 years in older women (p.1416-1418).
pitfalls: Not all NTM isolations, especially from the lung, reflect disease or require treatment; distinguishing colonization/contamination from true infection requires an appropriate clinical and radiographic setting (nodules, bronchiectasis, cavities) plus repeated isolation per American Thoracic Society criteria (p.1417).

The single most critical and sensitive step in diagnosis is simply to suspect NTM and request the correct, separately processed mycobacterial smears, cultures, and dedicated blood culture media; many cases go undiagnosed because the appropriate test was never ordered (p.1416-1417).
M. gordonae is frequently recovered from respiratory samples but is almost never a pathogen (p.1417).
PPD does not differentiate NTM from M. tuberculosis well; intermediate (~10 mm) reactions overlap, BCG cross-reacts, but large reactions (>15 mm) most commonly signify TB (p.1416-1417).

Slow-growing NTM typically do NOT proliferate in routine blood culture media, so suspicion and correct bottles are essential; biopsy isolation is strong evidence but laboratory contamination does occur (confirm with organisms on stained sections) (p.1417).
harrison.severityClassification: American Thoracic Society criteria for pulmonary NTM diagnosis: growth of NTM from two of three sputum samples (regardless of smear), OR a positive bronchoalveolar lavage sample (regardless of smear), OR a lung parenchymal biopsy with granulomatous inflammation or mycobacteria on section plus NTM on culture, in an appropriate clinical and radiographic setting. Isolation of NTM from blood or organ biopsy in a compatible clinical setting is considered diagnostic. NTM are categorized as rapidly growing (<7 days) versus slowly growing (>=7 days) (p.1417).
